records.place: Sonoma, Sonoma Valley, Sonoma County, California

wine.name: Hanzell Chardonnay
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone, grown on the estate.
wine.sites: The estate's hillside vineyards above Sonoma town, at the southern foot of the Mayacamas range, looking over the lower Sonoma Valley towards San Pablo Bay; its first Chardonnay vines went in here in 1953.
wine.making: Fermented largely in temperature controlled stainless steel, then aged in French oak barrels, a share of them new. Malolactic fermentation is held back for most of the wine, so it keeps much of its malic acid; by its own account the house adds no malolactic bacteria and filters the wine to keep that acid in the bottle.
wine.glass: Lemon peel, green apple and pear over hazelnut and a little toast, firm rather than broad, with taut acidity and a long, nutty finish; age brings honey and toasted bread.
wine.ageing: Tight and firm in its first years, it needs time in bottle and can keep for decades in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for half an hour if it seems closed; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The American Viticultural Area, or AVA, around Sonoma town; Sonoma County and Sonoma Coast are other, wider names.
The estate's name, joining Hana, the founder's wife, with the family name Zellerbach.

records.table: Planted in 1953 by an American industrialist who wanted Burgundy in Sonoma, the hillside estate above Sonoma town gives Hanzell Chardonnay. Fermented largely in steel and aged in French oak, it is firm and nutty and rewards years in bottle.
records.story: James D. Zellerbach (1892 to 1963), a paper industrialist who admired the wines of Burgundy, set out to make their like in Sonoma. In 1953 he planted his first vines, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, on the hillside above Sonoma town, and he named the estate Hanzell for his wife, Hana. The small winery that followed, of redwood and local stone, was modelled on the press house of the Clos de Vougeot, and the first vintage, on the house's timeline, came in 1957, the year he went to Rome as ambassador to Italy. With his founding winemaker he brought in small barrels of French oak, rare in California then, and temperature controlled fermenters of stainless steel. After Zellerbach died in 1963 his widow sold the stock, and much of the wine in barrel and bottle went to Heitz Cellar in Napa. The Day family bought and reopened the estate in the mid 1960s, and in 1975 it passed to the de Brye family. A winemaker hired in 1973 stayed until 2001 and held to the firm, long lived style. Hanzell is the estate credited with bringing the small French barrel and the cooled steel tank to California wine.

others.name: Hanzell Sebella Chardonnay
others.note: Another estate Chardonnay, fermented in stainless steel and aged six months in older French oak barrels.

others.name: Hanzell Pinot Noir

traps: Hanzell's Chardonnay is labelled Sonoma Valley; Sonoma County and Sonoma Coast are wider, different appellations.
The Ambassador's 1953 Vineyard names the original block, planted with Chardonnay and Pinot Noir in 1953, not a vintage.
Hanzell's Chardonnay sees French oak yet keeps much of its malic acid, so it is not a broad, fully malolactic wine in the manner of Kistler.

cards.front: Which Burgundy building gave the model for the Hanzell winery?

questions.q: Hanzell Chardonnay strikes a guest as leaner and more taut than many oaked California Chardonnays. Which part of its making explains it?
opts: Malolactic fermentation held back for most of the wine
Fermentation entirely in new American oak barrels
Long contact with the skins before pressing
Grapes drawn from cool Sonoma Coast ridges
questions.exp: Hanzell holds back malolactic fermentation for most of the wine, so it keeps its malic acid; it is aged in French oak, not American, and its vines grow in Sonoma Valley, not on the Sonoma Coast.

questions.q: After the founder of Hanzell died in 1963, his widow sold the wine in the cellar. Which Napa house bought much of it?

Beaulieu Vineyard
Inglenook
Charles Krug
questions.exp: Heitz Cellar bought much of the Hanzell wine in barrel and bottle that the founder left; the accounts of the sale name no other Napa house.

The first vintage is 1957 on the estate's timeline and in Decanter's, 1956 in some accounts; the Day family's purchase is 1965 in Wikipedia and 1966 in Wine Spectator, so the story says the mid 1960s.
The founding winemaker's controlled malolactic and inert gas work rest on Wine Spectator's pages alone, so the story keeps only the barrels and the steel, which the library also gives.
The library's holdings line calls the Ambassador's 1953 Vineyard among the oldest Chardonnay and Pinot Noir plantings; the estate's own pages tie that block to a Pinot Noir.

records.place: Vine Hill, Russian River Valley, Sonoma County, California

wine.name: Kistler Vineyard Chardonnay
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone, of the one heritage California selection the house plants in all its vineyards.
wine.sites: The Kistler Vineyard, the house's original planting, in a small bowl high on the western edge of the Mayacamas above Sonoma Valley, on Moon Mountain; the vines are dry farmed on St George rootstock.
wine.making: Fermented, the house says, by the native yeasts of its underground barrel cellars, in French barrels coopered at Saint-Romain in Burgundy from staves the house buys and air dries for about three years. The wine goes through full malolactic fermentation and rests long on its lees before bottling.
wine.glass: Hazelnut, lemon curd and baked pear over buttered toast, broad and creamy from the lees, yet held together by bright acidity through a long finish.
wine.ageing: Generous young, and a good year deepens over the following decade.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though a young bottle opens with air in the glass; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The house's original estate vineyard in the Mayacamas, bottled on its own since the 1986 vintage.
The valley's appellation; the vineyard lies in its eastern hills.

records.table: From the house's original vines, high in the Mayacamas above Sonoma Valley, Kistler Vineyard Chardonnay has been bottled on its own since 1986. Native yeasts ferment it in French barrels, and full malolactic gives it breadth, hazelnut and lemon curd kept fresh by its acidity.
records.story: Kistler was founded in 1978 by a winemaker and a partner, on the notion, as the house puts it, that California should make wines of site. Its first vintage was 1979. Its original winery stood high in the Mayacamas, above Sonoma Valley east of Glen Ellen, and the partners planted their own vineyard on that range in the house's first years. From the 1986 vintage that vineyard was bottled on its own, one of a row of Chardonnays each named for a single site, among them Dutton Ranch, Durell and McCrea, that made the single vineyard California Chardonnay a wine to collect. In the early 1990s the house outgrew the mountain and moved west to Vine Hill Road in the Russian River Valley, where it had planted vines of its own. By its own account Kistler plants one heritage selection of Chardonnay in every vineyard and ferments with native yeasts in French barrels, so that the site rather than the recipe marks each wine. The founding winemaker stepped down as chief executive at the end of 2017. To pour the Kistler Vineyard is to taste the house's rich, Burgundian Chardonnay at its source, the mountain where it began.

opts: Full malolactic fermentation and long ageing on its lees
A share of Viognier blended in from the estate
Fermentation in steel with malolactic held back
Grapes dried on mats before pressing

questions.exp: The original vineyard has been bottled on its own since the 1986 vintage; 1979 was the house's first vintage, and the move west to Vine Hill Road came in the early 1990s.

records.place: Westside Road, Healdsburg, Russian River Valley, Sonoma County, California

wine.name: Williams Selyem Rochioli Riverblock Vineyard Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, from several clones in the block, among them Pommard, 115 and 777 and a selection from Rochioli's West Block.
wine.sites: The River Block of the Rochioli family's vineyard on Westside Road, on gentle, mostly flat ground of Yolo sandy loam on the bank of the Russian River, where cool breezes meet well drained ground.
wine.making: Fermented in stainless steel dairy tanks, the vessel the founders took up early for its ratio of skins to juice and the house has kept, then aged for about sixteen months in barrels, about two thirds to four fifths of them new and the rest a year old, by the house's notes for the vintages of 2018 to 2024.
wine.glass: Black cherry, raspberry and pomegranate over cola, forest floor and a lift of rose petal, silky in texture, with fine tannin and juicy acidity.
wine.ageing: Open and sappy when young, and a good vintage gains forest floor and dried cherry over a decade.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant only an old bottle, off its sediment; a wide Burgundy glass.

label.means: The River Block of the Rochioli vineyard on Westside Road, a grower's site the house buys from.
The appellation of the river's cool lower valley in Sonoma County.

records.table: Rochioli fruit made the name of Williams Selyem in the 1980s, and its Rochioli Riverblock Pinot Noir grows in the riverside block of that vineyard on Westside Road. It pours silky, with black cherry, cola and forest floor.
records.story: Two friends began making wine for fun in a garage in the Russian River Valley in the late 1970s, starting with Zinfandel, and sold their first wines under the name Hacienda del Rio. In the early 1980s they made their first Pinot Noir, from grapes grown by the Rochioli family on Westside Road, who had begun planting Pinot Noir there in 1968. The founders soon put their own surnames on the label, and the 1984 vintage was the first called Williams Selyem. A year later came the wine that made them: the 1985 Rochioli Vineyard Pinot Noir won the sweepstakes prize at the California State Fair of 1987 against more than two thousand wines. Demand outran the little garage, and a waiting list to join the house's mailing list followed. At the end of the 1980s a Westside Road grower built them a plain winery on his ranch, and they moved in among the vineyards they bought from. The founders sold the house in 1998. In 2021 the Burgundy house of Faiveley took a minority stake, and in 2024 a majority. The Rochioli Riverblock leads back to the beginning: the house made its name on this vineyard's fruit, and the riverside block is where that fruit grows.

others.name: Allen Vineyard Pinot Noir
others.note: From the neighbouring Westside Road vineyard of the grower who built the founders a winery at the end of the 1980s.

others.name: Williams Selyem Zinfandel

The Allen vineyard on Westside Road

No source read calls the Rochioli Riverblock the house's flagship: the wine that made its name is the 1985 Rochioli Vineyard Pinot Noir (the house, Wine Spectator, a Substack history), and Riverblock is the Rochioli block the house bottles on its own, so the pick is kept as its Rochioli wine and the plan's why should say the Rochioli fruit, not the valley, made the name.

The Riverblock's planting year is left out: a house note gives 1989 for an old river block from cuttings of 1960s vines, yet the house also lists a 1988 Riverblock, and one account says the name changed in 1998.

The founders are not named: one died in 2019 by the house's pages and Decanter, with no birth year in two sources, and the other's status was not found; the Dyson couple of 1998, the Faiveley family members and every winemaker are living and kept out.

The library's style line speaks of a soft whole cluster perfume, while one account (a writer's own site, not cited) says the Pinot Noirs were largely destemmed and fermented with a yeast the house isolated; the making therefore says neither.

wine.name: Jordan Cabernet Sauvignon
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, about three quarters to four fifths, with Merlot, Petit Verdot and a little Malbec, and in some years a touch of Cabernet Franc.
wine.sites: Growers' vineyards across Alexander Valley, on the valley floor, the benchland and the hillsides, with hillside vines on the estate itself; the house turned to them after phylloxera struck its own valley floor vineyard in the 1990s. Some vintages take a little fruit from Mendocino County or Dry Creek Valley.
wine.making: Aged for about thirteen months in barrels, somewhat under half of them new, by the house's recent notes; it has been aged in French oak alone since the 2015 vintage, while the first, of 1976, was aged half in American oak. The wine then rests in bottle at the winery and is released about four years after the harvest, as the 1976 was released in 1980.
wine.glass: Blackcurrant and red cherry over cedar, tobacco leaf and dried herbs, medium bodied rather than heavy, with polished tannin and acidity enough to suit it to the table.
wine.ageing: Ready to drink on release, it holds and softens for a decade or more when the year is good.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; an hour in a decanter helps a young bottle; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: A warm valley appellation in northern Sonoma County, known for rounder Cabernet.
The house's full name, on the label of its Cabernet and of its Chardonnay.

records.table: Alexander Valley's Jordan Vineyard & Winery, founded in 1972 and built in the manner of a French château, makes one red: Jordan Cabernet Sauvignon. Mostly Cabernet with Merlot and Petit Verdot, held in barrel and bottle before release, it stays medium bodied and leaves room for the meal.
records.story: The estates of France inspired the couple who founded Jordan in 1972: they bought land in Alexander Valley near Healdsburg and planted Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot on the valley floor. To advise them they hired André Tchelistcheff (1901 to 1994), who had shaped Beaulieu in Napa, and he set the house on a French course. Building of the château began in the mid 1970s, and its cellar was finished a week before the harvest of 1976, the first Jordan Cabernet Sauvignon, which was released in 1980. A Chardonnay followed, and the house kept to those two wines. The winemaker who made that first vintage stayed until 2019. After phylloxera struck its valley floor vines in the 1990s, Jordan turned to growers across the valley and to hillside fruit, which its winemaker found more intense, and planted hillside vines on its own estate. The founders' son took over the running of the house in 2005, and in 2021 it bought another Alexander Valley vineyard. Jordan Cabernet is a study in balance: medium bodied, aged before release and built to partner food, not to overpower it.

others.name: Jordan Chardonnay
others.note: The house's one white, a Russian River Valley Chardonnay.

traps: Jordan Cabernet is labelled Alexander Valley, not Napa Valley; the house is in Sonoma County, across the Mayacamas from Napa.

wine.name: Seghesio Home Ranch Zinfandel
wine.grapes: Zinfandel, the great majority, with a small share of Petite Sirah.
wine.sites: The Home Ranch in Alexander Valley, where the founder planted Zinfandel in 1895; as the house tells it, the oldest vines grow near the family's Victorian house at the foot of Rattlesnake Hill.
wine.making: Picked by hand, sorted and destemmed into small open fermenters, the grapes steep for nine to twelve days with gentle punch downs and no pumping over. The free run wine finishes its malolactic fermentation in barrel and ages for twelve to fifteen months, mostly in neutral French and American oak with a little new French oak, by the house's notes.
wine.glass: Black raspberry, bramble and blackberry jam with black pepper and clove, ripe and round, with soft tannin and a warm, peppery finish.
wine.ageing: Most vivid in its first years, while the fruit is bright; a strong vintage keeps and softens for a decade.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The family's first vineyard, in Alexander Valley, planted to Zinfandel in 1895.
The ranch's appellation, in northern Sonoma County; Dry Creek Valley is a separate one.

records.table: In 1895 a winemaker from Piedmont and his wife planted the Alexander Valley vineyard that gives Seghesio Home Ranch Zinfandel. With a little Petite Sirah and mostly older barrels, it runs ripe, peppery and round, a red for the grill.
records.story: The founder left Piedmont for Sonoma County in 1886 to work as a winemaker at the Italian Swiss Colony. In 1895 he and his wife bought a stretch of Alexander Valley and planted Zinfandel there, the vineyard the family calls the Home Ranch. He kept his post at the Colony until 1902, when he finished a winery of his own, and his vines came through Prohibition. Long a seller of bulk wine, the family released wines under the Seghesio name only in 1983. Early in the 1990s the family cut its output sharply and turned to wines from the vineyards it farmed, Zinfandel above all. The Home Ranch Zinfandel is the wine the house builds around the vines of 1895. Crimson Wine Group bought the business from the family in 2011, and family members stayed on for a time in the cellar and the vineyards. Home Ranch shows what an Italian family's Zinfandel planting can become over more than a century.

others.name: Seghesio Sonoma Zinfandel
others.note: A Zinfandel blended from several vineyards and labelled Sonoma County, the house's broader bottling.

traps: The Home Ranch lies in Alexander Valley, while the winery stands in Healdsburg; the label names Alexander Valley.
Petite Sirah in the blend is not Syrah: it is Durif, a separate grape long grown among California's Zinfandel.

cards.front: Seghesio: when did the family first bottle wine under its own name?
cards.back: In 1983; for decades before, the family sold its wine in bulk.

cards.front: Seghesio's Home Ranch: beside which house and hill do its old Zinfandel vines grow?
cards.back: The family's Victorian house, at the foot of Rattlesnake Hill in Alexander Valley.

questions.q: How is Seghesio Home Ranch Zinfandel raised before bottling, by the house's own notes?
opts: Twelve to fifteen months, mostly in neutral oak barrels
Three years in new American oak hogsheads
Six months in stainless steel tanks alone
Many years in a solera of old casks
questions.exp: The house's sheets give twelve to fifteen months in barrel, mostly neutral French and American oak with a little new French; it is neither raised in steel alone nor in a solera.

questions.q: The founder of Seghesio came from Piedmont in 1886 to make wine in Sonoma County. Where did he work until 1902?
opts: The Italian Swiss Colony
The Buena Vista winery
The Inglenook estate
The Fountaingrove colony
questions.exp: He was a winemaker at the Italian Swiss Colony until 1902, when he finished his own winery; Buena Vista, Inglenook and Fountaingrove play no part in the family's story.

report: The house is not in the library; the founding of 1895 rests on the house's own pages, the Sonoma County Winegrowers' profile and Forbes, the move of 1886 and the post at the Italian Swiss Colony until the winery of 1902 on several accounts (North Bay Biz, the house's legacy page, Wine Geeks).
The founder and his wife are described, not named: their dates were found in no source.
Home Ranch as the house's leading Zinfandel rests on the house (built around the founders' vines of 1895), Liberty Wines and Drinkhacker; the pick is kept.
The cut of the early 1990s rests on the Sonoma County Winegrowers (1993) and Cigar Aficionado (1994); the debt behind it is Cigar Aficionado's alone and is left out.

The sale of 2011 rests on Wine Spectator and the Sonoma County Winegrowers; that family members stayed on rests on the Winegrowers and the buyer's own release of 2015, which is not cited because its address names a living person.
Left out for want of a second source: the Chianti Station Sangiovese of 1910, the acreage of 1895 and the claim that the family crushed half the county's red grapes.
The making, the blend and the barrels come from the house's sheets for 2015, 2020, 2021 and 2022; no respelling of Seghesio was found in a source, so say is empty.

changed: story, cards[0]: 1983 is the first release under the family name, which included a blend of 1975 made by the third generation, so the fourth generation is cut (the house's newsletter and Marian's Reserve page, BKWine).
story: family members stayed on after the sale of 2011 for a time, a family winemaker having since left for a label of his own (Press Democrat).
questions[0]: the key is twelve to fifteen months, as the house's sheets and the explanation give, no longer about fifteen.
open: The purchase of 1895 against a house bought in 1893; the marriage in 1893 or 1894; neither is in the record.
One account has the founder and his wife owning the Italian Swiss Colony itself in 1919 and 1920; not added for want of a second source.
